notes: Built now: the committee's monthly public report lists payments to the candidate (the purpose stays private); outlets see it through the ordinary news desk; a rival reads it and decides whether to complain; the state regulator's own review of reports opens a matter when nobody complains; a campaign bookkeeper who already raised a payment privately and finds another decides whether to complain outside the campaign.
Not built: an outside accountant or auditor, a reporter investigating beyond the public record, the FEC's own review of federal reports, prosecutors.
The filing lag (30 days) and report interval (30 days) are authored, not law.

title: Who actually catches a candidate spending campaign money on themselves
usableAnswer: For federal and for state campaigns: the discovery routes with their rough share of cases and typical time from spending to discovery, sourced; whether filings name the candidate as payee; and which routes the game is missing.
whyItMatters: The owner defined this as done when reporters, an accountant, the FEC or regulator, or someone inside the campaign can notice. The routes now exist with authored timing; the timing and weighting should be real.

answer.summary: ChatGPT mapped the federal detection routes and procedural stages and found no source for any route-share percentage, typical discovery delay, or direct-payee versus intermediary split. Routes: public disclosure and outside scrutiny; a sworn complaint from any person (no special opponent route); Reports Analysis Division review and referral to the Office of General Counsel or ADR; the FEC Audit Division (example: the Raul Ruiz for Congress 2018 interim audit); other agency referrals; DOJ criminal referral, which needs knowing-and-willful intent. Payees are itemized once they pass $200 per election cycle; House and Senate committees file quarterly plus pre-election reports. Matters stay confidential while pending; the public file appears generally 30 days after certification of the closing vote. Eight stages: transaction, evidence, lead, complaint or referral, reason to believe, investigation, probable cause, litigation. Fixed FEC clocks: notice 5 days, response 15, pre-probable-cause conciliation 60, post-probable-cause conciliation 30 to 90. It warns: do not turn a complaint into a guilt finding or use one universal discovery probability.

answer.stillOpen: Open: exact state detection procedures were 'not verified across all 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico'; route percentages, discovery delays, reason-to-believe and investigation durations are unknown. Not supportable: state route percentages, a universal delay, a uniform payee pattern, any single 30-day interval or penalty range. Four decisions it leaves pending: a 52-jurisdiction legal-source pass; whether route-incidence calibration is needed at all (possibly a coded sample of closed FEC matters); how to treat campaign accountants; not using 'reason to believe' or 'probable cause' labels in states that do not use them. Its design implications are 'possible game-model choices, not empirical rates or legal requirements.'
